analysisDescription: The game is a very cooperative game in which players have to maintain a good communication and it is really the main focus of the game. It allows the players to die and, if the other is alive, the other goes instantly back to life. I have played this game multiple times and it is a good game for a couple or friends. I used the paper of the living framework for understading cooperative games to gain knowledge and examples that helped me analyze this game.

dimensionExamples.example: The players have to do tasks in a sequential order, working together, mainly in a coordinated manner to progress.

dimension.title: Sequential Collaboration
dimension.description: In sequential collaboration, players have to do tasks in sequential order, with tasks typically assigned to different players.

dimensionExamples.example: Players communication is required is this game so that they can coordinate their actions, it is essential to have a good communication to complete the tasks in the game. This communication can be in real life or using other software that provides in real-time communication.

dimension.title: Required/Incentivised
dimension.description: When Required/Incentivised, the game challenges require players to communicate (e.g. when there is essential asymmetric information), or incentivised through challenges that are made easier through it (e.g. coordinating combined actions for maximum effect).

dimensionExamples.example: Players can play in the same machine, but also have the ability to create a party online with a partner.

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: The objective of this game is to pass the multiple stages of the game, where players advance together.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example: In this game there is a few mini-games in which the players can compete with each other, but it does not affect the goal of the game.

dimension.title: Conflicting
dimension.description: Conflicting goals are also observable in some cooperative games, where typically, players compete in certain sections that do not affect the overarching goal of the game. While no semi-cooperative games were observed, in these types of games, conflicting goals can also be mixed with shared goals

dimensionExamples.example: The players have to surpass different phases of the game, so they can advance to the next one. In this 2-player game, they always go together.

dimension.title: Party
dimension.description: Party progression results from the contributions of a group of players that opted to play together, where part of the progress is solely associated with that group (not shared with the rest of the server or community).

dimensionExamples.example: Each player takes control of one of the two characters in the game.

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: In this game there are only two characters to be chosen, in the game, they have different abilities to complement each other.

dimension.title: Pool
dimension.description: Pool describes when players are given an array of playable entities to choose from (e.g. characters, nations, class). These have predefined gameplay characteristics and in some cases, players can be forced to have a unique selection.

dimensionExamples.example: The progress of each player identity is predefined by the storyline.

dimension.title: Predefined
dimension.description: When progress is strictly linear, with no player choice (e.g., dictated by the storyline, predefined upgrades or progressing through switching entities)

dimensionExamples.example: The players are teammates and they need to both cooperate to surpass each stage of the game.

dimension.title: Teammates
dimension.description: Teammates, where players within a team need to coordinate their actions, abilities, and roles in order to reach a common goal against at least another team.

dimensionExamples.example: In the mini-games, the players compete with each other to see who takes the casual win, that does not have influence in the story of the game.

dimension.title: Competitors
dimension.description: Competitors, where you may be able to compete with other players, either momentarily or through the whole game session (e.g. team vs team match-based games).

dimensionExamples.example: The players interact within the same world.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimensionExamples.example: When players play in the same screen, each player has a viewpoint of its character.

dimension.title: Split
dimension.description: Split typically divides the view by the number of players, with each being associated with a particular section. Players will have a smaller view of the game world as a result, but they will still be able to experience different game areas from the perspective of the other player. Similarly, this usually happens in co-located experiences with a single physical screen.

dimensionExamples.example: The players usually do different tasks that compliment each other's task, so they both can progress.

dimension.title: Coupled Collaboration
dimension.description: In coupled collaboration, players take on different tasks that somehow intertwine and typically contribute to a shared outcome.

dimensionExamples.example: Players have to do tasks/perform actions in parallel.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: It is possible for players to use their characters to shoot something to inform the other player of the task/action they have to perform.

dimension.title: In-Game Movement/Actions
dimension.description: Players can communicate through specific movement or actions (e.g. shooting a weapon on the ground to notify others to pick it up)

dimensionExamples.example: One player is dependent of the other player tasks and actions to advance in the game.

dimension.title: Task
dimension.description: Task refers to gameplay tasks where at least one player is dependent on another. These can force players to coordinate to be effective and complete them.

dimensionExamples.example: In this game both have to cooperate so they can both achieve success and surpass the challenges.

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimensionExamples.example: The players rely on each other.

dimension.title: Playable characters
dimension.description: Playable characters refer to every entity within the environment whose actions are controlled by player input. As mentioned before, the locus of control may differ from game to game, but usually, each player controls one playable character. Playable characters are shared when their state and actions can be assumed by more than one player. This may happen in different ways: 1) shared representation; 2) manipulating partner’s entity; 3) switching between playable characters of a shared pool.

dimensionExamples.example: The player control characters with different abilities, most of which complement with the other.

dimension.title: Abilities
dimension.description: Abilities, as described by Harris et al. 2016, are where one player can do things another player cannot. In games where these actions synergise or are complementary, it incentivises collaboration.

dimensionExamples.example: This value of the game is shared, and their abilities complement each other, for example, one shoots nails and the other can support it self in the nails.

dimension.title: Complementarity
dimension.description: Complementarity, extended from Rocha et. al rocha2008game, corresponds to when player actions are designed to balance each other’s weaknesses or so that strengths complement each other. It is typically achieved through asymmetric game design, with each player bringing something to the shared experience.
